In enterprise Java applications, hardcoding database credentials, cryptographic keys, and API tokens into application properties files or relying on insecure practices is a major vulnerability vector. Secrets management addresses this lifecycle by centralizing, encrypting, and auditing sensitive configurations separate from the source code. HashiCorp Vault acts as an enterprise-grade, backend-agnostic secrets engine offering dynamic secrets, lease renewals, and robust revocation. AWS Secrets Manager provides a cloud-native solution tightly integrated with the AWS IAM ecosystem, featuring automatic database credential rotation out of the box. Meanwhile, injecting secrets via environment variables—while ubiquitous and supported natively by Spring Boot's PropertySource abstraction—suffers from severe limitations such as leakage via process lists (ps aux), lack of audit trails, and exposure in crash-dump logs.

Spring Cloud Vault and Spring Cloud AWS bridge these external vaults directly into the Spring Environment during the application bootstrap phase. By leveraging BootstrapContext and PropertySourceLocators, Spring fetches secrets before the core ApplicationContext initializes, injecting them seamlessly into @Value or Environment abstractions without developers needing to write custom HTTP client boilerplate to fetch tokens from Vault or AWS APIs.

rows: AWS KMS-backed encryption, IAM access policies
Custom and built-in dynamic lease revocation
Native automatic rotation via Lambda functions
CloudTrail integration for API call tracking

items: Spring Boot evaluates externalized configuration during the EnvironmentPostProcessor phase, allowing Spring Cloud Vault or AWS Secrets Manager to populate properties prior to bean instantiation.
HashiCorp Vault employs dynamic secret generation, creating short-lived database credentials on demand that automatically expire after a configured lease time-to-live (TTL).
AWS Secrets Manager integrates with AWS IAM roles for tasks, allowing ECS containers or EC2 instances to authenticate without storing static AWS access keys on the filesystem.

    secrets:
      databaseCredentials: myapp/db-creds

A classic production gotcha when using environment variables or fetching remote secrets is accidental exposure through actuators or logging. If a Spring Boot Actuator endpoint like `/actuator/env` is left unsecured or improperly filtered, it will dump all resolved properties—including decrypted secrets fetched from Vault or AWS—in plain text to any caller. Always ensure sensitive keys are explicitly masked using management.endpoint.env.keys-to-sanitizer.
